learningObjectives.title: The sales process and customer service

questions.q: Which production method involves making a single, one-off, unique product to a customer's specific requirements?
options: Job production
Batch production
Flow production
Lean production
questions.explain: Job production makes one unique item at a time, such as a tailored suit or a bespoke wedding cake.

questions.q: In flow production, products are:
options: Produced continuously in large quantities on an assembly line
Made one at a time as unique items
Made in groups before the process is changed to a different item
Produced only after an individual customer places an order
questions.explain: Flow production continuously mass-produces large quantities of identical products, often on an automated assembly line.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a key feature of batch production?
options: A group of identical products is made before the process switches to a different batch
Each item is individually designed for a single customer
Products move continuously along a line and never stop
Only one finished product is ever completed at a time
questions.explain: Batch production makes a group (batch) of identical items, then changes the setup to make a different batch, such as different flavours of bread.

questions.q: A benefit of just-in-time (JIT) stock management is that it:
options: Reduces the cost of holding and storing stock
Guarantees the business can never run out of stock
Removes the need to rely on any suppliers
Increases the amount of buffer stock held
questions.explain: JIT delivers materials only as they are needed, so little stock is held and storage costs are reduced.

questions.q: A bakery makes 200 identical loaves, then cleans the equipment and makes 150 identical bread rolls. Which production method is this?
options: Batch production
Job production
Flow production
Lean production
questions.explain: Making one group of identical items and then switching to make a different group is batch production.

questions.q: Quality control (QC) usually involves:
options: Inspecting products at the end of the production process to find faults
Making every worker responsible for building in quality throughout
Preventing all errors before any production begins
Removing the need for any checking of products
questions.explain: Quality control relies on inspecting or testing products, typically at the end of production, to identify defective items.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation TQM stand for?
options: Total Quality Management
Timed Quality Method
Total Quantity Measurement
Team Quality Monitoring
questions.explain: TQM (Total Quality Management) is an approach where quality is the responsibility of everyone in the business.

questions.q: How does quality assurance differ from quality control?
options: Quality assurance builds quality in throughout the process rather than only inspecting the finished product
Quality assurance only checks products once they are completed
Quality assurance removes all workers from the production process
Quality assurance ignores customer expectations entirely
questions.explain: Quality assurance aims to prevent faults by ensuring quality at every stage, whereas quality control mainly inspects at the end.

questions.q: Why is maintaining good quality important for a business?
options: It helps build a strong reputation and encourages repeat custom
It always reduces the selling price to zero
It removes the need for any marketing
It guarantees the business pays no tax
questions.explain: Consistent quality builds customer trust and reputation, leading to repeat purchases and fewer costly returns.

questions.q: A clothing manufacturer trains every employee to check and correct their own work as they go, rather than only inspecting finished garments. This is an example of:
options: Quality assurance
Quality control
Flow production
Procurement
questions.explain: Making quality the responsibility of every worker throughout the process is a quality assurance approach.

questions.q: Which of the following is an element of good customer service in the sales process?
options: Staff having good product knowledge
Deliberately slow service
Ignoring all customer feedback
Refusing to offer any after-sales support
questions.explain: Good product knowledge lets staff answer questions and recommend suitable products, a key part of good customer service.

questions.q: The term 'post-sales service' refers to:
options: Support offered to customers after they have bought a product
The price charged before a product is sold
The advertising shown before a purchase
The production of the product itself
questions.explain: Post-sales service is support given after purchase, such as warranties, helplines or repairs.

questions.q: A likely benefit to a business of providing good customer service is:
options: Increased customer loyalty and repeat purchases
Higher raw material costs
A steady fall in total sales
A weaker business reputation
questions.explain: Good customer service builds loyalty, encouraging customers to return and recommend the business to others.

questions.q: Why is staff product knowledge important during the sales process?
options: It helps staff answer questions and recommend suitable products, increasing sales
It deliberately slows down the service given to customers
It removes the need for the business to hold any stock
It reduces the quality of the products sold
questions.explain: Knowledgeable staff can match products to customer needs and build confidence, helping to close sales.

questions.q: After buying a laptop, a customer is given a warranty and access to a technical helpline. These are examples of:
options: Post-sales service
Quality control
Flow production
Procurement
questions.explain: Warranties and helplines are support provided after the sale, so they are post-sales service.

questions.q: What is procurement?
options: The process of finding and buying goods and services from suppliers
The process of selling finished products to customers
The process of designing a new product
The process of advertising a product to the public
questions.explain: Procurement is sourcing and purchasing the materials, goods and services a business needs from its suppliers.

questions.q: On a stock control (bar gate stock) graph, the 're-order level' is:
options: The stock level at which a new order for stock is placed
The maximum amount of stock the business can hold
The point at which the business has zero stock left
The total amount of stock sold in a year
questions.explain: The re-order level is the point at which fresh stock is ordered so it arrives before stock runs out.

questions.q: Which of these is an important factor when a business chooses a supplier?
options: The quality and reliability of the goods supplied
The supplier owner's favourite colour
Whether the supplier has a large car park
The number of pets owned by employees
questions.explain: Businesses judge suppliers on factors such as quality, reliability, cost, delivery speed and availability.

questions.q: Why might a business choose to hold a level of buffer stock?
options: To avoid running out of stock if demand rises or deliveries are delayed
To deliberately increase its storage costs
To stop selling products to customers
To reduce the quality of its products
questions.explain: Buffer stock is a minimum reserve kept to cope with unexpected demand or late deliveries and avoid stock-outs.

questions.q: A supermarket arranges daily deliveries so that it holds very little stock in its warehouse. Which stock approach is this?
options: Just in time (JIT)
Just in case
Job production
Quality control
questions.explain: Receiving frequent deliveries and holding minimal stock is the just-in-time (JIT) approach to stock management.
